title: Boundaries, Part 1: The Method and Two Questions

beats.say: Boundaries questions ask you to choose the punctuation that correctly connects, or separates, the parts of a sentence.
The choices are usually the same words, with different punctuation. They might be a comma, a semicolon, a colon, a dash, a period, or nothing at all.
The whole topic depends on one skill. You must tell an independent clause from a dependent clause.
An independent clause has a subject and a verb, and it can stand alone as a sentence. The museum opened in eighteen ninety.
A dependent clause can't stand alone. Because the museum opened, isn't a full sentence.
Which the museum displays, is also dependent. Words like because and which make a clause depend on something else.
Step one. Look at the choices, and see what changes. Is it a comma, a semicolon, a colon, or a period?
beats.item: See what changes in the choices

beats.say: Step two. Find the boundary, and ask whether the part before it's an independent clause. Then ask the same about the part after.
beats.item: Is each side an independent clause?

beats.say: Step three. If both sides are independent, use a period, a semicolon, or a comma with and, but, or so. If not, usually use a comma, or nothing.
Step four. Look for extra information that needs matching marks on both sides.
Two independent clauses are joined by a period, or a semicolon. A semicolon works just like a period.
They can also be joined by a comma followed by a conjunction such as and, but, or so.
A colon follows a complete independent clause. What comes after the colon explains or lists.
Extra information needs matching marks on both sides, two commas or two dashes, never one of each.
Finally, never put any punctuation between a subject and its verb, even when the subject is long.
Easy question. We split the sentence at the blank, and ask whether each side can stand alone.

scenes.title: Read the sentence
scenes.text: The orchestra rehearsed for six weeks before the concert ______ the performance sold out within an hour.

beats.say: The part before the blank is complete. The orchestra rehearsed for six weeks before the concert. It's an independent clause.
The part after the blank is also complete. The performance sold out within an hour. So we're joining two independent clauses.

scenes.title: Which punctuation fits?
scenes.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

beats.say: Choice A uses only a comma. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses. That's a comma splice.
Choice B uses nothing at all, which joins two clauses with no mark. That's a run-on.
Choice D adds a comma after and. That second comma is unnecessary, and it breaks the sentence.
Choice C uses a semicolon, which correctly joins two independent clauses. The answer is C.
Medium question. Extra information inside a sentence is set off by matching marks. If it opens with a comma, it must close with a comma.

card.text: Open with a comma, close with a comma

scenes.title: Read the sentence
scenes.text: The town's oldest building, a stone mill constructed in 1782 ______ still uses its original water wheel to grind grain for local bakeries.

beats.say: The core sentence is, the town's oldest building still uses its original water wheel. That's the main idea.
beats.underline: still uses its original water wheel

beats.say: A stone mill constructed in seventeen eighty-two, is extra information. It opened with a comma after building, so it must close with a comma.

scenes.title: Which punctuation fits?
scenes.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

beats.say: Choice A uses a semicolon. A semicolon would cut the subject off from its verb, so it can't work.
Choice B uses no mark. Then the extra information is left open on one side, and the pair is unbalanced.
Choice C uses a dash. A dash doesn't match the opening comma, so the pair is mismatched.
Choice D closes the pair with a comma, so the extra information has matching marks. The answer is D.
To recap. Find the boundary, and ask whether each side is an independent clause. Two independent clauses need a period or a semicolon.
Extra information needs matching marks. In the next video, we work through a hard question and the common traps.
